newsitem.title: USA: Murder trial to reveal seamy side of U.S. TV shows.
newsitem.headline: Murder trial to reveal seamy side of U.S. TV shows.

text.p: The seamy side of U.S. daytime talk shows may be as much on trial as the defendant in a murder case starting on Monday involving the shotgun killing of a homosexual after a fantasy television expose.

Jonathan Schmitz is accused of gunning down Scott Amedure, 32, three days after Amedure surprised him by appearing on a taping of the "Jenny Jones" syndicated television show on March 6, 1995, as his homosexual secret admirer.

After more than a year of delays, lawyers in the trial known as the "Jenny Jones" case, start selecting the jury in Oakland County Circuit Court in Pontiac, Michigan, on Monday that will decide the fate of Schmitz, 25, from the Detroit suburb of Lake Orion.

Schmitz, who says he is a heterosexual, claims he was tricked into appearing on the Chicago-based show and humiliated during a taping that would have aired on national television. The taped show was never shown.
Before Schmitz walked onto the set of the show, which was airing people's fantasies about those they secretly admire, audience members were treated to a description of Amedure's fantasy for Schmitz.

Prompted by Jones, Amedure said his fantasy involved whipped cream, strawberries and champagne, according to Schmitz attorney James Burdick. One producer allegedly wrote in notes: "I think Jon is going to die when he sees it's Scott," Burdick said.
That Schmitz killed Amedure is not in dispute. He confessed to the crime on a 911 emergency call to police shortly after firing two shotgun blasts into Amedure at close-range.

Schmitz's lawyers argue he was in a suicidal, diminished mental state when he bought the gun less than an hour before the killings. A suggestive note from Amedure that Schmitz found on his doorstep the morning of the killing pushed him past the breaking point, Burdick said.
"The furthest thing from Jonathan's mind was to shoot anybody other than himself," said Burdick.

Jenny Jones, a perky, blonde-haired diva of the daytime talk show set, will not appear in court. The Michigan State Court of Appeals disagreed with defence attorneys who wanted her to testify in front of the jury, ruling that a taped deposition from Jones was sufficient.
Burdick accuses Jones of ducking her responsibility. "The last thing in the world she wants is to own up to this," says Burdick.
Burdick says he obtained producer and script notes that reveal Jones and her staff were more concerned with entertaining the audience than treating guests fairly.

Barbara Brogliatti, a spokeswoman for Telepictures Productions, unit of Warner Bros., which produces the show, declined to comment. She cited a judge's order barring potential witnesses from discussing the case, and repeated the show's position that it was not at fault.
"We don't believe the show is responsible for this tragedy," said Brogliatti.

The case has been marked by numerous delays and sensational twists. Both prosecutors and defence attorneys took the extremely unusual step last summer of asking the Michigan State Court of Appeals to remove Oakland County Circuit Judge Francis X. O'Brien from the case. The appeals court refused.

In August 1995, Scott Amedure's family hired Geoffrey Fieger, the lawyer made famous by representing assisted suicide crusader Dr. Jack Kevorkian, and filed a $25 million lawsuit against the Jenny Jones Show, Telepictures and Warner Bros.
The family alleges the show enticed Amedure to create fantasies involving Schmitz, provided him with alcohol before the show and urged him to provoke a strong audience reaction.
Prosecutors could not be reached for comment on the trial. Attorneys expect it to last one month.
